Why wispack hand-rolls its own forking

forking.Rmd

wisp()’s bootstrap-resampling step (bs_batch(), implemented in src/wspc.cpp and src/fork_utils.h) distributes many independent per-resample model fits – each an NLopt optimization over a Stan Math autodiff model – across forked child processes, rather than using base R’s parallel::mclapply(). A CRAN reviewer may reasonably ask why a package forks its own processes at the C++ level instead of calling a standard, already-reviewed base-R parallelism primitive. This page is that justification, backed by a reproducible benchmark rather than assertion.

Short answer: for the small models in this package’s own tests and tutorials, mclapply() is actually a little faster. For the large models this package is designed for in practice (the kind of fit a user runs with 1,000+ parameters and many bootstraps), the result reverses – mclapply() becomes measurably slower, and uses measurably more peak memory, because its long-lived worker processes accumulate heap-allocator-retained memory across many sequential bootstrap fits. The hand-rolled forking code avoids this because it forks a fresh batch of short-lived children for every batch of resamples; each child’s entire address space, including whatever it allocated, is reclaimed by the OS the moment it exits. Memory safety at the scale this package targets, not just raw speed, is the reason for the custom implementation.

The comparison

Both the hand-rolled path and the mclapply() alternative are variations on the same idea: fork worker processes, have each do some share of the bootstrap resampling, and collect the results back in the parent. They differ in process lifetime:

  • fork_utils.h’s run_forked_batches() forks a fresh batch of up to max.fork children for every batch of resamples. A child does its one resample’s fit, writes its result back through a pipe, and calls _exit(). The next batch forks brand-new children from the parent’s own (bounded) memory state – not from whatever the previous batch’s children had grown their heaps to.
  • parallel::mclapply(mc.preschedule = TRUE) forks exactly mc.cores workers once, and each worker processes its entire assigned share of the task list sequentially, in-process, before exiting.

Two benchmarks compare them directly, holding everything else fixed: same underlying cpp_model object (freshly initialized, not yet fit), same bootstrap count, same number of workers, nothing else running in either arm. The real bs_batch() production path is one arm; mclapply() over the package’s internal per-resample fit function is the other.

Result 1: a small, realistic model (276 parameters)

Using this package’s own liverradial tutorial/test fixture (882,144 simulated count-data rows, 276 fitted parameters – see tests/testthat/test-slow-liverradial.R and benchmarks/RESULTS.md for the full methodology and raw numbers):

bootstraps workers bs_batch() mclapply() mclapply vs. bs_batch()
100 2 137.1s 130.2s 1.05x faster
100 10 33.7s 32.1s 1.05x faster
1000 20 189.0s 157.1s 1.20x faster

At this scale, mclapply() is consistently 5-20% faster. The reason is simple: each fork in fork_utils.h costs a fork() syscall plus pipe setup/teardown (sub-millisecond to low-single-digit milliseconds), and bs_batch() pays that cost on every one of the 1,000 bootstraps, while mclapply() pays its (slightly different) fixed per-worker cost only once per worker. At ~0.15-0.3s of real optimization work per bootstrap, that per-fork overhead is a real, if modest, fraction of total time.

Taken in isolation, this result would argue for switching to mclapply(). It does not tell the whole story.

Result 2: a large model (4,788 parameters), the regime this package is actually built for

The package’s own author has, outside of testing, fit models with 1,000+ parameters that collectively use 50+ GB of RAM across concurrent bootstrap fits – a regime the 276-parameter benchmark above does not probe. To test whether the result above generalizes, the same benchmark was repeated on a 4,788-parameter model built from this package’s real multi-context tutorial data (ACx_laminar_countdata_demo_with_celltype.csv.gz, keeping 12 of the data’s 31 real MapMyCells cell types instead of the tutorial’s own simplifying collapse to 2 – no fabricated data; see benchmarks/RESULTS_large_model.md for full methodology):

bootstraps workers bs_batch() mclapply() mclapply vs. bs_batch()
20 4 204.3s 224.3s 0.91x (9% slower)
20 10 125.8s 136.7s 0.92x (8% slower)
20 20 104.5s 124.7s 0.84x (16% slower)
40 20 138.7s 148.0s 0.94x (6% slower)

The result reverses completely. Every grid point flips sign: bs_batch() is now consistently faster than mclapply(), by 6-16%.

Peak combined memory (RSS, summed across all worker processes) shows why:

bootstraps workers bs_batch() peak RSS mclapply() peak RSS ratio
20 4 15.5 GB 23.8 GB 1.54x
20 10 37.3 GB 41.0 GB 1.10x
40 20 57.7 GB 89.4 GB 1.55x

The clearest pattern: holding the number of workers fixed at 20 and doubling the bootstrap count from 20 to 40 (so each mclapply worker now does 2 sequential fits instead of 1 before exiting) makes mclapply’s peak RSS almost exactly double. bs_batch()’s peak RSS barely moves under the same change, because fork_utils.h forks an entirely fresh batch of children every batch regardless of how many total batches run.

Why: this is heap-allocator behavior, not a Stan memory leak

Both code paths correctly call clear_stan_mem() (stan::math::recover_memory()) after every individual bootstrap fit – bs_batch()’s serial path does this explicitly (src/wspc.cpp, bs_fit(b, true)), and the benchmark’s mclapply arm calls the identical exposed bs_fit() method. So this is not a case of Stan’s autodiff arena silently growing across calls within a worker; that is actively guarded against in both arms, on every call.

The accumulation is instead ordinary process-memory behavior: a long-lived process’s malloc implementation generally retains freed pages, mapped for reuse, rather than returning them to the OS immediately – especially for the large, variably-sized allocations a multi-thousand- parameter NLopt fit makes on every bootstrap resample. An mclapply worker that runs several such fits sequentially, in the same process, can retain a high-water-mark of these pages across its entire assigned sequence. A fork_utils.h child, by contrast, is a distinct OS process for exactly one bootstrap fit: when it calls _exit(), the OS reclaims its entire address space in one shot, freed-but-retained allocator pages included. The next batch’s freshly forked children start from the parent’s own bounded memory state, never from whatever the previous batch’s children grew their heaps to – regardless of how many total bootstraps the model asks for.

At 276 parameters, this same mechanism is present (mclapply’s RSS is higher there too, by 1.06-1.97x across configurations) but the absolute memory at stake is small enough that it costs nothing in wall-clock time; mclapply’s one-time-fork-cost advantage dominates instead. At 4,788 parameters, the same mechanism costs tens of gigabytes, which is large enough – more TLB/cache pressure, slower allocator searches, more OS paging – to flip the net timing result. For the even larger models (1,000+ parameters, 50+ GB combined across concurrent bootstraps) this package is actually used for, this is the regime that matters.

Conclusion

The hand-rolled forking in src/fork_utils.h is not a case of reinventing a wheel CRAN’s parallel package already provides for free. It is a deliberate choice, made because this package’s bootstrap-resampling workload – many repeated, memory-heavy Stan/NLopt fits, at model sizes that routinely reach the tens-of-gigabytes range in combined memory – sits in exactly the regime where long-lived worker processes accumulate retained memory in a way that short-lived, re-forked-every-batch children do not. The benchmark scripts (benchmarks/mclapply_vs_fork_general.R, benchmarks/configs/*.R) and raw results (benchmarks/RESULTS.md, benchmarks/RESULTS_large_model.md) are included in the repository so this comparison is reproducible rather than taken on faith.

This is not a criticism of parallel::mclapply(), which remains a better fit for workloads made of many short, memory-light tasks – precisely because it avoids fork_utils.h’s per-task fork overhead in that regime, as Result 1 shows. It is a statement that the right choice is workload-dependent, and this package’s own workload lands on the side that favors re-forking short-lived children over long-lived persistent workers.
